claim: DYT1 is a debilitating movement disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in torsinA.
source: DYT1 is a debilitating movement disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in torsinA.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Mouse models which have embryonically targeted torsinA have failed to recapitulate the dystonia seen in patients.
source: Mouse models which have embryonically targeted torsinA have failed to recapitulate the dystonia seen in patients, possibly due to differential developmental compensation between rodents and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction discussing various mouse models.

claim: TorsinA knockdown in the cerebellum, but not in the basal ganglia, was sufficient to induce dystonia.
source: TorsinA knockdown in the cerebellum, but not in the basal ganglia, was sufficient to induce dystonia.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: TorsinA knockdown in the immature cerebellum failed to produce dystonia.
source: In agreement with a potential developmental compensation for loss of torsinA in rodents, torsinA knockdown in the immature cerebellum failed to produce dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Abnormal motor symptoms in knockdown animals were associated with irregular cerebellar output caused by changes in the intrinsic activity of both Purkinje cells and neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Abnormal motor symptoms in knockdown animals were associated with irregular cerebellar output caused by changes in the intrinsic activity of both Purkinje cells and neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The onset of symptoms in DYT1 patients occurs before the age of 26 with a focal dystonia that often generalizes, resulting in severe disability.
source: The onset of symptoms in DYT1 patients occurs before the age of 26 with a focal dystonia that often generalizes, resulting in severe disability (Bressman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the clinical description.

claim: The majority of DYT1 patients share a single amino acid deletion in torsinA.
source: The majority of DYT1 patients share a single amino acid deletion in torsinA (Ozelius et al., 1997; Risch et al., 1995; Warner and Jarman, 1998), resulting in loss of function of the protein (Goodchild et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the genetic basis of DYT1.

claim: Studies in DYT1 patients have implicated the cerebellum in this disorder.
source: Studies in DYT1 patients have implicated several brain areas in this disorder, including the cerebellum (Eidelberg et al., 1998) and basal ganglia (Panov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Studies in DYT1 patients have implicated the basal ganglia in this disorder.
source: Studies in DYT1 patients have implicated several brain areas in this disorder, including the cerebellum (Eidelberg et al., 1998) and basal ganglia (Panov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to studies.

claim: Mice with complete knockout of torsinA exhibit early lethality.
source: Unfortunately, mice with complete knockout of torsinA exhibit early lethality and cannot be studied (Goodchild et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the observation.

claim: No viable rodent models of DYT1 show overt dystonia.
source: Further, no viable rodent models of DYT1 show overt dystonia (Dang et al., 2005; Goodchild et al., 2005; Grundmann et al., 2012, 2007; Page et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2005; Shashidharan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to previous mouse models.

claim: Brain region-specific genetic models of torsinA dysfunction do not show overt symptoms.
source: The same is true of brain region-specific genetic models of torsinA dysfunction (Liang et al., 2014; Pappas et al., 2015; Weisheit and Dauer, 2015; Yokoi et al., 2011, 2008; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to region-specific models.

claim: Two recently generated mouse models of DYT1 exhibited some twisting movements but do not exhibit the overt sustained postures common in dystonic patients.
source: While two recently generated mouse models of DYT1 exhibited some twisting movements (Liang et al., 2014), these mice do not exhibit the overt sustained postures common in dystonic patients.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to the specific models.

claim: There is high embryonic expression of torsinA in rodents.
source: But there is evidence that while there is high embryonic expression of the protein in rodents (Vasudevan et al., 2006; Xiao et al., 2004), it is only expressed postnatally in humans (Siegert et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to expression studies.

claim: TorsinA is only expressed postnatally in humans.
source: But there is evidence that while there is high embryonic expression of the protein in rodents (Vasudevan et al., 2006; Xiao et al., 2004), it is only expressed postnatally in humans (Siegert et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to human expression studies.

claim: Compensation of torsinA is highly likely in rodents, which could explain discrepancies between current DYT1 rodent models and patients with DYT1.
source: This suggests that compensation of torsinA is highly likely in rodents which could explain discrepancies between current DYT1 rodent models and patients with DYT1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on the differential expression patterns.

claim: Acute knockdown of the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ - ATPase pump in the cerebellum of adult rodents was sufficient to induce dystonia.
source: In fact, we previously showed in a mouse model of RDP that acute knockdown of the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ - ATPase pump in the cerebellum of adult rodents was sufficient to induce dystonia, whereas genetic mouse models targeting the gene early in development did not produce dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing prior work by the authors.

claim: Genetic mouse models targeting the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ - ATPase pump early in development did not produce dystonia.
source: In fact, we previously showed in a mouse model of RDP that acute knockdown of the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ - ATPase pump in the cerebellum of adult rodents was sufficient to induce dystonia, whereas genetic mouse models targeting the gene early in development did not produce dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing prior work.

claim: Mice with cerebellar knockdown of torsinA during the early post-natal period had mild symptoms with no dystonia.
source: In contrast, mice with cerebellar knockdown of torsinA during the early post-natal period had mild symptoms with no dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Compensation of torsinA in early rodent brain development can explain the major differences in phenotype between adults and juveniles after torsinA knockdown.
source: This observation suggests that indeed compensation of torsinA in early rodent brain development can explain the major differences in phenotype between adults and juveniles after torsinA knockdown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Abnormal cerebellar activity may be a common mechanism in some hereditary dystonias.
source: It is tempting based on these and previous findings (Fremont et al., 2015) to hypothesize that abnormal cerebellar activity may be a common mechanism in some hereditary dystonias.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis based on current and previous findings.

claim: Imaging studies have implicated the cerebellum in another inherited dystonia.
source: In fact, imaging studies have implicated the cerebellum in another inherited dystonia (Carbon et al., 2010a, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to imaging studies.

claim: AAV-TorsinAshRNA-GFP injection resulted in significant knockdown of torsinA in the basal ganglia (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.187 ± 0.06).
source: Significant knockdown of torsinA (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.187 ± 0.06) was achieved and post-mortem histology demonstrated robust expression throughout the injected areas (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C with western blot data.

claim: Animals injected with a shRNA against torsinA in the basal ganglia did not develop dystonia.
source: Animals injected with a shRNA against torsinA in the basal ganglia did not develop dystonia, as assessed by the dystonia scale.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: The behavior of mice with torsinA knockdown in the basal ganglia was similar to controls injected with a non-targeted shRNA.
source: Moreover, the behavior of the mice was similar to controls injected with a non-targeted shRNA (AAV-NTshRNA-GFP) (Figure 1D, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: Multiple parameters of open field behavior were unchanged in animals with knockdown of torsinA in the basal ganglia throughout the post-injection period.
source: Multiple parameters of open field behavior quantified in animals with knockdown of torsinA in the basal ganglia, including average velocity, steps taken in 30 s, distance travelled in 5 min and step size, were unchanged throughout the post-injection period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injection of AAV-torsinA shRNA-GFP into the cerebellum resulted in generalized expression of the construct.
source: Injection of AAV-torsinA shRNA-GFP resulted in generalized expression of the construct (Figure 1E) and significant knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.2214 ± 0.05) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Injection of AAV-torsinA shRNA-GFP into the cerebellum resulted in significant knockdown of torsinA (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.2214 ± 0.05).
source: Injection of AAV-torsinA shRNA-GFP resulted in generalized expression of the construct (Figure 1E) and significant knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.2214 ± 0.05) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1F with western blot data.

claim: Mice with acute knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum developed uncoordinated movements progressing to frequent dystonic postures.
source: Mice with acute knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum developed uncoordinated movements progressing to frequent dystonic postures (Figure 1G and Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G and Video 2.

claim: Injection of a second shRNA (AAV-TorsinA shRNA2-GFP) into the cerebellum resulted in comparable symptoms to the first shRNA.
source: In separate cohorts of mice, injection of a second shRNA (AAV-TorsinA shRNA2-GFP) resulted in comparable symptoms, while injection of AAV-NTshRNA-GFP to the same region had no effect on motor behavior (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G (note: text says Figure 1F but likely refers to 1G based on context).

claim: Injection of AAV-NTshRNA-GFP into the cerebellum had no effect on motor behavior.
source: In separate cohorts of mice, injection of a second shRNA (AAV-TorsinA shRNA2-GFP) resulted in comparable symptoms, while injection of AAV-NTshRNA-GFP to the same region had no effect on motor behavior (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In patients with dystonia, abnormal co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscle pairs often underlies abnormal postures.
source: In patients with dystonia, abnormal co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscle pairs often underlies abnormal postures (Frucht, 2013; Hughes and McLellan, 1985; Yanagisawa and Goto, 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to clinical studies.

claim: Electromyographic recordings in mice with torsinA KD in the cerebellum demonstrated that abnormal posturing of the hind limb is due to muscle co-contraction.
source: Electromyographic (EMG) recordings in mice with torsinA KD in the cerebellum demonstrated that abnormal posturing of the hind limb in these animals is due to muscle co-contraction, similar to what is seen in patients (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1H,I with EMG data.

claim: Knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum and basal ganglia did not enhance the severity of dystonia when compared to mice with torsinA KD in the cerebellum alone.
source: We found that knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum and basal ganglia did not enhance the severity of dystonia when compared to mice with torsinA KD in the cerebellum alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The severity of dystonic symptoms correlated with the extent of torsinA knockdown.
source: It was noted that the severity of dystonic symptoms correlated with the extent of knockdown, such that as knockdown increased so did the severity of symptoms.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1J.

claim: When torsinA protein level was knocked down by at least 60% dystonic symptoms were observed.
source: When torsinA protein level was knocked down by at least 60% dystonic symptoms were observed (Figure 1J, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1J with statistical analysis.

claim: A substantial decrease in torsinA protein levels is necessary to produce dystonia.
source: From these data, it is clear that a substantial decrease in torsinA protein levels is necessary to produce dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the dose-response data.

claim: DCN neurons from dystonic torsinA KD animals fired abnormally with bursts of action potentials.
source: Recordings from deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) neurons, which comprise the majority of the cerebellar output, revealed that these cells fired abnormally with bursts of action potentials, whereas DCN cells in controls (NTshRNA) fired tonically (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A with electrophysiological traces.

claim: DCN cells in controls fired tonically.
source: Recordings from deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) neurons, which comprise the majority of the cerebellar output, revealed that these cells fired abnormally with bursts of action potentials, whereas DCN cells in controls (NTshRNA) fired tonically (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The average firing rate of DCN neurons from dystonic animals was nearly half that of controls (control: 55.5 ± 4.1 sp/s, dystonic: 22.4 ± 3.4 sp/s, p<0.00001).
source: Further, the average firing rate of DCN neurons from dystonic animals was nearly half that of controls (Figure 2B, control average firing rate: 55.5 ± 4.1 spikes/second (sp/s), average firing rate in dystonic mice: 22.4 ± 3.4 sp/s, p<0.00001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B with quantification.

claim: An increase in the irregularity of cerebellar output can underlie ataxia.
source: It has been shown that an increase in the irregularity of cerebellar output can underlie ataxia (Walter et al., 2006) and in some cases dystonia in rodents (Fremont et al., 2014, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior studies.

claim: An increase in the irregularity of cerebellar output can underlie dystonia in rodents.
source: It has been shown that an increase in the irregularity of cerebellar output can underlie ataxia (Walter et al., 2006) and in some cases dystonia in rodents (Fremont et al., 2014, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior studies.

claim: The CV ISI of DCN neurons recorded from dystonic animals was nearly triple that of controls (control: 0.55 ± 0.03, dystonic: 1.53 ± 0.13, p<0.00001).
source: However, the CV ISI of DCN neurons recorded from dystonic animals was nearly triple that of controls, despite the decrease in average firing rate, suggesting that the activity of these neurons is highly erratic (Figure 2C, control CV ISI: 0.55 ± 0.03, dystonic CV ISI: 1.53 ± 0.13, p<0.00001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C with quantification.

claim: There was a trend towards an increase in the PFR of DCN cells recorded from dystonic mice with torsinA KD compared to controls (control: 77.3 ± 5.7 sp/s, dystonic: 105.1 ± 22.3 sp/s, p=0.21).
source: There was a trend towards an increase in the PFR of DCN cells recorded from dystonic mice with torsinA KD compared to controls, (Figure 2D, control: 77.3 ± 5.7 sp/s, dystonic animals: 105.1 ± 22.3 sp/s, p=0.21), and there was a peak in the ISI histogram of DCN neurons from dystonic mice at shorter interspike intervals around 2 ms (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D with quantification.

claim: There was a peak in the ISI histogram of DCN neurons from dystonic mice at shorter interspike intervals around 2 ms.
source: There was a trend towards an increase in the PFR of DCN cells recorded from dystonic mice with torsinA KD compared to controls, (Figure 2D, control: 77.3 ± 5.7 sp/s, dystonic animals: 105.1 ± 22.3 sp/s, p=0.21), and there was a peak in the ISI histogram of DCN neurons from dystonic mice at shorter interspike intervals around 2 ms (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Dystonia in mice with torsinA KD is caused by abnormal and erratic cerebellar output.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that dystonia in mice with torsinA KD is caused by abnormal and erratic cerebellar output.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Purkinje cells fire regularly in vivo under normal conditions.
source: Normally, Purkinje cells fire regularly in vivo but in dystonic animals Purkinje cells exhibited abnormal bursting activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is established knowledge about Purkinje cell physiology.

claim: In dystonic animals Purkinje cells exhibited abnormal bursting activity.
source: Normally, Purkinje cells fire regularly in vivo but in dystonic animals Purkinje cells exhibited abnormal bursting activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F with electrophysiological traces.

claim: There was no significant difference between the average firing rate of Purkinje cells from dystonic mice and those from controls (control: 69.1 ± 5.3 sp/s, dystonia: 51.1 ± 12.1 sp/s, p=0.13).
source: There was no significant difference between the average firing rate of Purkinje cells from dystonic mice (torsinA KD) and those from controls (NTshRNA) (Figure 2G, control: 69.1 ± 5.3 sp/s, dystonia: 51.1 ± 12.1 sp/s, p=0.13).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2G with quantification.

claim: The CV ISI of Purkinje cells from dystonic animals was increased by over two-fold compared to controls (control: 0.05 ± 0.03, dystonia: 1.21 ± 0.12, p<0.0001).
source: However, the CV ISI of Purkinje cells from dystonic animals was increased by over two-fold compared to controls (Figure 2I, control: 0.05 ± 0.03, dystonia: 1.21 ± 0.12, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2I with quantification.

claim: The PFR of Purkinje cells from torsinA KD animals was significantly increased (control: 85.7 ± 7.1 sp/s, dystonia: 124.6 ± 22.5 sp/s, p=0.031).
source: The PFR of Purkinje cells from torsinA KD animals was also significantly increased (Figure 2H, control: 85.7 ± 7.1 sp/s, dystonia: 124.6 ± 22.5 sp/s, p=0.031).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2H with quantification.

claim: Aberrant Purkinje cell output caused by knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum could contribute to the abnormal activity of DCN neurons.
source: These findings suggest that aberrent Purkinje cell output caused by knockdown of torsinA in the cerebellum could contribute to the abnormal activity of DCN neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Purkinje cells are intrinsically active pacemaking neurons that fire regular action potentials even when deprived of synaptic input.
source: Purkinje cells are intrinsically active pacemaking neurons that fire regular action potentials even when deprived of synaptic input (Batini and Kado, 1967; Bell and Grimm, 1969; Latham and Paul, 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to classic studies on Purkinje cell physiology.

claim: Purkinje cells have high expression of torsinA.
source: Since Purkinje cells have high expression of torsinA, alterations in this activity resulting from torsinA KD could contribute to the changes in Purkinje cell firing reported above (Konakova et al., 2001; Puglisi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to expression studies.

claim: TorsinA KD altered the intrinsic activity of Purkinje cells, converting their pacemaking to irregular burst firing.
source: TorsinA KD altered the intrinsic activity of Purkinje cells, converting their pacemaking to irregular burst firing.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Purkinje cells with torsinA KD had an average firing rate similar to NT and WT (WT: 53.9 ± 6.7, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 68.1 ± 13.1 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.8 ± 7.0 sp/s, p=0.45).
source: Although Purkinje cells with torsinA KD had an average firing rate similar to NT and WT (average firing rate of WT: 53.9 ± 6.7, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 68.1 ± 13.1 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.8 ± 7.0 sp/s, p=0.45, Figure 3B), the PFR was nearly doubled (PFR of WT: 53.7 ± 6.6, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 93.2 ± 20.7 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.5 ± 6.9 sp/s, p=0.048, Figure 3C) and the CV ISI was increased by ~10 fold (CV ISI of WT: 0.110 ± 0.010, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 1.151 ± 0.248, NT GFP+: 0.096 ± 0.008, p=0.0003, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B with quantification.

claim: The PFR of Purkinje cells with torsinA KD was nearly doubled (WT: 53.7 ± 6.6, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 93.2 ± 20.7 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.5 ± 6.9 sp/s, p=0.048).
source: Although Purkinje cells with torsinA KD had an average firing rate similar to NT and WT (average firing rate of WT: 53.9 ± 6.7, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 68.1 ± 13.1 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.8 ± 7.0 sp/s, p=0.45, Figure 3B), the PFR was nearly doubled (PFR of WT: 53.7 ± 6.6, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 93.2 ± 20.7 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.5 ± 6.9 sp/s, p=0.048, Figure 3C) and the CV ISI was increased by ~10 fold (CV ISI of WT: 0.110 ± 0.010, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 1.151 ± 0.248, NT GFP+: 0.096 ± 0.008, p=0.0003, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C with quantification.

claim: The CV ISI of Purkinje cells with torsinA KD was increased by ~10 fold (WT: 0.110 ± 0.010, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 1.151 ± 0.248, NT GFP+: 0.096 ± 0.008, p=0.0003).
source: Although Purkinje cells with torsinA KD had an average firing rate similar to NT and WT (average firing rate of WT: 53.9 ± 6.7, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 68.1 ± 13.1 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.8 ± 7.0 sp/s, p=0.45, Figure 3B), the PFR was nearly doubled (PFR of WT: 53.7 ± 6.6, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 93.2 ± 20.7 sp/s, NT GFP+: 49.5 ± 6.9 sp/s, p=0.048, Figure 3C) and the CV ISI was increased by ~10 fold (CV ISI of WT: 0.110 ± 0.010, GFP+ TorsinA KD: 1.151 ± 0.248, NT GFP+: 0.096 ± 0.008, p=0.0003, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D with quantification.

claim: GFP− Purkinje cells from dystonic animals had similar firing patterns compared to those from wild-type and AAV9-NTshRNA-GFP controls.
source: GFP− Purkinje cells from dystonic animals had similar firing patterns compared to those from wild-type and AAV9-NTshRNA-GFP controls (Figure 3B,C,D,E), providing evidence that torsinA knockdown affects the intrinsic pacemaking of these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B,C,D,E.

claim: Knockdown of torsinA disrupts the intrinsic activity of Purkinje cells.
source: Together, these findings suggest that knockdown of torsinA disrupts the intrinsic activity of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the in vitro electrophysiology data.

claim: DCN neurons are intrinsically active, pacemaking cells with high expression of torsinA.
source: DCN neurons are also intrinsically active, pacemaking cells with high expression of torsinA (Konakova et al., 2001; Puglisi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to expression studies.

claim: Knockdown of torsinA alters the normal tonic activity of DCN neurons, causing them to fire at lower rates and with bursts.
source: In vitro recordings of the intrinsic activity of DCN neurons, with fast glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic transmission blocked, demonstrated that knockdown of torsinA alters the normal tonic activity of these neurons, causing them to fire at lower rates and with bursts (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3F with electrophysiological traces.

claim: DCN neurons from GFP+ areas of torsinA shRNA injected animals had a mean average firing rate nearly half that of the controls (GFP+ dystonic: 7.9 ± 2.3 sp/s, GFP+ control: 21 ± 2.1 sp/s, p=0.0011).
source: DCN neurons from GFP+ areas of torsinA shRNA injected animals had a mean average firing rate nearly half that of the controls (GFP+ neurons from dystonic animals: 7.9 ± 2.3 sp/s, p=0.0011, GFP+ neurons from control animals: 21 ± 2.1 sp/s, Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3G with quantification.

claim: DCN neurons recorded from GFP+ areas in slices from dystonic mice exhibited a ten-fold increase in the CV ISI compared to controls (GFP+ dystonic: 1.21 ± 0.312, GFP+ control: 0.1 ± 0.011, p=0.0021).
source: Further, DCN neurons recorded from GFP+ areas in slices from dystonic mice exhibited a ten-fold increase in the CV ISI compared to controls (GFP+ neurons from dystonic animals: 1.21 ± 0.312, GFP+ neurons from control animals: 0.1 ± 0.011, p=0.0021, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3I with quantification.

claim: There was a trend towards an increased PFR in DCN neurons with torsinA KD, but it was not statistically significant (GFP+ TorsinA: 41.9 ± 14.2 sp/s, GFP+ NT DCN: 21.4 ± 2.2 sp/s, p=0.15).
source: Although there was a trend towards an increased PFR in neurons with torsinA KD, it was not statistically significant (GFP+ TorsinA: 41.9 ± 14.2 sp/s, GFP+ NT DCN: 21.4 ± 2.2 sp/s, p=0.15, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3H with quantification.

claim: Knockdown of torsinA in the adult mouse cerebellum affects the intrinsic activity of at least two populations of cerebellar neurons, Purkinje cells and neurons of the DCN.
source: These combined in vitro electrophysiological findings suggest that knockdown of torsinA in the adult mouse cerebellum affects the intrinsic activity of at least two populations of cerebellar neurons, Purkinje cells and neurons of the DCN, likely contributing to dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the in vitro electrophysiology data.

claim: Patients with DYT1 exhibit no gross morphological changes in the brain.
source: Although patients with DYT1 exhibit no gross morphological changes in the brain, there may be more subtle cell loss in certain brain areas (McNaught et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to a patient study.

claim: There may be subtle cell loss in certain brain areas in patients with DYT1.
source: Although patients with DYT1 exhibit no gross morphological changes in the brain, there may be more subtle cell loss in certain brain areas (McNaught et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: Rodent models of DYT1 suggest that loss of torsinA results in apoptosis and gliosis in particular regions including the cerebellum.
source: Further, rodent models of DYT1 suggest that loss of torsinA results in apoptosis and gliosis in particular regions including the cerebellum (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to a rodent model study.

claim: An increase in apoptotic cells was identified in dystonic mice compared to control animals injected with a non-targeted shRNA.
source: An increase in apoptotic cells was identified in dystonic mice compared to control animals injected with a non-targeted shRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A with TUNEL staining.

claim: Cell death was comparable in the cerebellar cortex of control animals injected with the non-targeting (NT) shRNA and those with torsinA knockdown (NT: 4.3 ± 0.95, torsinA KD: 3.53 ± 0.54).
source: Interestingly, even though both Purkinje cells and DCN neurons were found to intrinsically fire abnormally in the dystonic mice, cell death was comparable in the cerebellar cortex of control animals injected with the non-targeting (NT) shRNA and those with torsinA knockdown (Percent cell death in torsinA KD mice: 3.53 ± 0.54 compared to NT shRNA mice: 4.3 ± 0.95) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B with quantification.

claim: There was noticeable cell death in the DCN of mice with torsinA KD (torsinA KD: 12.59 ± 1.54, NT: 5.43 ± 1.14).
source: However, there was noticeable cell death in the DCN of mice with torsinA KD (Percent cell death in torsinA KD mice: 12.59 ± 1.54 compared to NT shRNA mice: 5.43 ± 1.14).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B with quantification.

claim: Significant cell death in the DCN was observed up to 200 µm away from the injection site in the torsinA injected animals but not in the NT injected mice.
source: Nonetheless, significant cell death in the DCN was observed up to 200 µm away from the injection site in the torsinA injected animals but not in the NT injected mice (Figure 4C), suggesting that the DCN is sensitive to dysfunction of torsinA and that loss of torsinA can lead to DCN cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C with quantification.

claim: The DCN is sensitive to dysfunction of torsinA.
source: Nonetheless, significant cell death in the DCN was observed up to 200 µm away from the injection site in the torsinA injected animals but not in the NT injected mice (Figure 4C), suggesting that the DCN is sensitive to dysfunction of torsinA and that loss of torsinA can lead to DCN cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the cell death data.

claim: Loss of torsinA can lead to DCN cell death.
source: Nonetheless, significant cell death in the DCN was observed up to 200 µm away from the injection site in the torsinA injected animals but not in the NT injected mice (Figure 4C), suggesting that the DCN is sensitive to dysfunction of torsinA and that loss of torsinA can lead to DCN cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the cell death data.

claim: The difference in symptoms reported for mice with embryonic knockout of torsinA in the hind brain and those with acute knockdown of torsinA in the adult is notable.
source: The difference in symptoms reported for mice with embryonic knockout of torsinA in the hind brain (Liang et al., 2014) and those with acute knockdown of torsinA in the adult is notable.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation comparing different models.

claim: Mice with conditional knockout of torsinA in the cerebellum and midbrain using an En1-cre mouse line were mildly ataxic.
source: Mice with conditional knockout of torsinA and mice with a conditional knock-in of torsinA in the cerebellum and midbrain using an En1-cre mouse line were mildly ataxic (Liang et al., 2014), whereas mice with torsinA KD in the adult mouse cerebellum developed overt dystonic postures.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to the specific model.

claim: The motor abnormalities of the En1-cre selective knock-in mice attenuated over time.
source: Interestingly, the motor abnormalities of the En1-cre selective knock-in mice attenuated over time (Liang et al., 2014), suggesting a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: Purkinje cells continue their maturation after birth up to 28 days postnatally.
source: Purkinje cells continue their maturation after birth up to 28 days postnatally and granule cells undergo enormous proliferation during this time (Hatten and Heintz, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to a developmental study.

claim: Granule cells undergo enormous proliferation during the early postnatal period.
source: Purkinje cells continue their maturation after birth up to 28 days postnatally and granule cells undergo enormous proliferation during this time (Hatten and Heintz, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: Mice injected with AAV-TorsinA shRNA-GFP at postnatal day 7 showed knockdown of torsinA (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.16 ± 0.025) comparable to that seen in mice injected as adults.
source: These animals showed knockdown of torsinA (average torsinA levels after KD: 0.16 ± 0.025) comparable to that seen in mice injected as adults (Figure 5B—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B—figure supplement 1 with western blot data.

claim: Mice injected with torsinA shRNA in the early postnatal period developed only mild motor symptoms and no dystonia, regardless of the level of knockdown.
source: However, unlike mice injected in adulthood, mice injected in the early postnatal period developed only mild motor symptoms and no dystonia, regardless of the level of knockdown (Figure 5C, Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C and Video 3.

claim: Mice compensate for knockdown of torsinA during development.
source: This finding suggests that mice compensate for knockdown of torsinA during development, and it may explain, at least in part, why the development of dystonic animal models of DYT1 has been challenging.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the developmental knockdown data.

claim: Differences in compensation for knockdown between adult and developing animals has been shown for other neuronal proteins.
source: Differences in compensation for knockdown between adult and developing animals has also been shown for other neuronal proteins (Mallucci et al., 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2010; Nerbonne et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to other studies.

claim: In patients with DYT1, onset of dystonia usually occurs in childhood/early adolescence, with an average age of onset of 12.
source: It is interesting to note that in patients with DYT1, onset of dystonia usually occurs in childhood/early adolescence, the average age of onset is 12, (Bressman, 2004) in which most of the brain development has occurred.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to a clinical study.

claim: By acutely knocking down torsinA in the cerebellum of adult mice, the authors generated an animal model that faithfully replicates the symptoms and features of DYT1.
source: By acutely knocking down the protein implicated in DYT1 in adult mice, we generated an animal model that faithfully replicates the symptoms and features of this disorder.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the main finding.

claim: Knockdown of torsinA gradually produces severe and overt dystonia.
source: We find that knockdown of torsinA gradually produces severe and overt dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The cerebellum and not the basal ganglia is implicated as the main site of dysfunction in DYT1 dystonia.
source: Remarkably, the cerebellum and not the basal ganglia is implicated as the main site of dysfunction in DYT1 dystonia.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a key conclusion from the study.

claim: Dystonias are the third most common movement disorder.
source: Although dystonias are the third most common movement disorder we currently have few, if any, effective therapies (Balint and Bhatia, 2014; Stacy, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: We currently have few, if any, effective therapies for dystonia.
source: Although dystonias are the third most common movement disorder we currently have few, if any, effective therapies (Balint and Bhatia, 2014; Stacy, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: A sizable fraction of dystonias are hereditary and are caused by mutations in a variety of different genes.
source: A sizable fraction of dystonias are hereditary and are caused by mutations in a variety of different genes (Bressman, 2004; Charlesworth et al., 2013; Klein et al., 1999; Müller, 2009; Németh, 2002; Nygaard et al., 1999; Paudel et al., 2012; Risch et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: In most cases, DYT1 is caused by a 3 bp deletion in the torsin1A gene, resulting in the loss of a single glutamate residue in the C-terminus of the protein torsinA.
source: In most cases, DYT1 is caused by a 3 bp deletion in the torsin1A gene, resulting in the loss of a single glutamate residue in the C-terminus of the protein torsinA (Ozelius and Lubarr, 1993; Ozelius et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: The DYT1 mutation causes little, if any, notable neurodegeneration.
source: Because this mutation causes little, if any, notable neurodegeneration in DYT1, it is thought that dystonia results from dysfunction of neurons (Konakova et al., 2001; McNaught et al., 2004; Rostasy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: It is thought that dystonia in DYT1 results from dysfunction of neurons.
source: Because this mutation causes little, if any, notable neurodegeneration in DYT1, it is thought that dystonia results from dysfunction of neurons (Konakova et al., 2001; McNaught et al., 2004; Rostasy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: TorsinA is a member of the AAA-ATPase family of proteins.
source: TorsinA is a member of the AAA-ATPase family of proteins and is likely to have a number of different functions in the cell (Neuwald et al., 1999; Vale, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: TorsinA is likely to have a number of different functions in the cell.
source: TorsinA is a member of the AAA-ATPase family of proteins and is likely to have a number of different functions in the cell (Neuwald et al., 1999; Vale, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: There are numerous examples where acutely disrupting the function of a protein in mice has major consequences, but knockout of the same gene manifests as few, if any, discernable outcomes.
source: To underscore this point, it is noteworthy that there are numerous examples where acutely disrupting the function of a protein in mice has major consequences, but knockout of the same gene manifests as few, if any, discernable outcomes (Daude et al., 2012; De Souza et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2013; Hommel et al., 2003; Rossdeutsch et al., 2012; Rossi et al., 2015; White et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: There are a number of studies which demonstrate that the effect of knockdown or knockout of a particular protein in the brain can be dependent on when that protein is lost.
source: In fact, there are now a number of studies which demonstrate that the effect of knockdown or knockout of a particular protein in the brain can be dependent on when that protein is lost (Erdmann et al., 2007; Mallucci et al., 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2010; Nerbonne et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2003; Yuan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: In RDP, subjects carrying the mutation often lead a relatively healthy life until they are exposed to a very stressful event, at which point they rapidly develop severe dystonia and Parkinsonism-like symptoms.
source: In RDP, subjects carrying the mutation often lead a relatively healthy life until they are exposed to a very stressful event, at which point they rapidly develop severe dystonia and Parkinsonism-like symptoms (Brashear et al., 2007, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to clinical descriptions of RDP.

claim: Transgenic mice harboring loss of function mutations in the Na/K pump have generally failed to exhibit overt dystonia.
source: Similar to other mouse models of hereditary dystonias, transgenic mice harboring loss of function mutations in the Na/K pump have generally failed to exhibit overt dystonia (Clapcote et al., 2009; DeAndrade et al., 2011; Moseley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: Partially blocking the function of the Na/K pump in the basal ganglia and the cerebellum of adult mice resulted in mild motor dysfunction.
source: While partially blocking the function of the Na/K pump in the basal ganglia and the cerebellum of adult mice resulted in mild motor dysfunction, stressing these mice precipitated severe dystonia and Parkinsonism-like symptoms that persisted thereafter (Calderon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to the RDP model.

claim: Stressing mice with partial Na/K pump blockade precipitated severe dystonia and Parkinsonism-like symptoms that persisted thereafter.
source: While partially blocking the function of the Na/K pump in the basal ganglia and the cerebellum of adult mice resulted in mild motor dysfunction, stressing these mice precipitated severe dystonia and Parkinsonism-like symptoms that persisted thereafter (Calderon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Dystonia in the RDP mouse model was instigated by the dysfunction of the cerebellum.
source: Further scrutiny of this mouse model surprisingly revealed that dystonia was instigated by the dysfunction of the cerebellum, whereas the Parkinsonism-like features were of basal ganglia origin (Calderon et al., 2011; Fremont et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to the RDP model studies.

claim: The Parkinsonism-like features in the RDP mouse model were of basal ganglia origin.
source: Further scrutiny of this mouse model surprisingly revealed that dystonia was instigated by the dysfunction of the cerebellum, whereas the Parkinsonism-like features were of basal ganglia origin (Calderon et al., 2011; Fremont et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: Recent postmortem histological studies have identified cerebellar degeneration in RDP.
source: The relevance of this finding to the human disorder has been strengthened by the fact that recent postmortem histological studies have identified cerebellar degeneration in RDP (Sweadner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: In some patients mutations in the Na/K pump can result in Adult Rapid Onset Ataxia rather than dystonia.
source: Moreover, it has also been recently reported that in some patients mutations in the Na/K pump can result in Adult Rapid Onset Ataxia rather than dystonia (Sweadner et al., 2016), a finding that highlights the role of the cerebellum in the disorder and further validates the pharmacologic and shRNA mouse models.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: The level of torsinA transcript and protein in neural tissue is markedly different between the developing mouse and human brain.
source: This is because expression studies demonstrate that the level of torsinA transcript and protein in neural tissue is markedly different between the developing mouse and human brain (Siegert et al., 2005; Vasudevan et al., 2006; Xiao et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to expression studies.

claim: In humans torsinA protein is not detectable in neurons until one month after birth when expression abruptly increases to levels maintained throughout adulthood.
source: In humans torsinA protein is not detectable in neurons until one month after birth when expression abruptly increases to levels maintained throughout adulthood (Siegert et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: In the rodent brain torsinA is present at high levels embryonically and peaks during the early postnatal period, decreasing rapidly within a couple of weeks postnatally before stabilizing.
source: In contrast, in the rodent brain torsinA is present at high levels embryonically and peaks during the early postnatal period, decreasing rapidly within a couple of weeks postnatally before stabilizing (Vasudevan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: The most symptomatic transgenic mouse models to date exhibiting mild abnormal twisting movements were generated using Nestin-cre mice.
source: Indeed, the most symptomatic transgenic mouse models to date exhibiting mild abnormal twisting movements were generated using Nestin-cre mice (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Recombination begins at E11 in Nestin-cre mice but increases gradually until early postnatal life.
source: Even though recombination begins at E11 in Nestin-cre mice, it increases gradually until early postnatal life, which temporally delays neuronal torsinA dysfunction during the gestation period (Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: TorsinB is a related homologue to torsinA with 70% homology.
source: One of these proteins, torsinB, is a related homologue to torsinA with 70% homology (Ozelius et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Both torsinA and torsinB proteins are localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope membrane system in cells throughout the brain and non-neural cells.
source: Both torsinA and torsinB proteins are localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope membrane system in cells throughout the brain and non-neural cells (Naismith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: In DYT1 KI and KO mice, nuclear envelope budding was observed only in neurons in the CNS and no nuclear envelope budding was found in non-neuronal cells or in non-CNS tissue.
source: In DYT1 KI and KO mice, nuclear envelope budding was observed only in neurons in the CNS and no nuclear envelope budding was found in non-neuronal cells or in non-CNS tissue even though torsinA is expressed in all these tissues (Goodchild et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: When torsinB was knocked down in fibroblasts from a DYT1 mutant background, nuclear envelope defects were seen in non-neuronal cells as well.
source: However, when torsinB was knocked down in fibroblasts from a DYT1 mutant background, nuclear envelope defects were seen in non-neuronal cells as well, demonstrating that torsinB can compensate for loss of torsinA (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: TorsinB can compensate for loss of torsinA.
source: However, when torsinB was knocked down in fibroblasts from a DYT1 mutant background, nuclear envelope defects were seen in non-neuronal cells as well, demonstrating that torsinB can compensate for loss of torsinA (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Either torsinA or torsinB can individually rescue the abnormal nuclear envelope budding when embryoid body cells are differentiated into neural lineage.
source: To determine whether a similar compensation can occur in the CNS, Tanabe et al used embryoid bodies derived from DYT1 KI animals and showed that either torsinA or torsinB can individually rescue the abnormal nuclear envelope budding when the cells are differentiated into neural lineage (Tanabe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Torsin2A appeared to rescue nuclear envelope budding to some extent.
source: Interestingly, torsin2A also appeared to rescue nuclear envelope budding to some extent (Tanabe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Expression of torsinB like torsinA, differs temporally between mice and humans.
source: It is also noteworthy that expression of torsinB like torsinA, differs temporally between mice and humans (Siegert et al., 2005; Tanabe et al., 2016; Vasudevan et al., 2006) adding yet another level of complication to modeling DYT1 in rodents.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: DYT1 has partial (30–40%) penetrance in humans.
source: It is tempting to speculate that perhaps some of the same compensatory mechanisms, alas not as effectively or on every occasion, might be engaged in humans and might account for the partial (30–40%) penetrance of DYT1 in humans (Argyelan et al., 2009; Eidelberg et al., 1998; Martino et al., 2013; Ozelius and Lubarr, 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: For a number of years neuroimaging studies in patients with DYT1 have hinted that the cerebellum is involved in dystonia.
source: For a number of years neuroimaging studies in patients with DYT1 have hinted that the cerebellum is involved in dystonia (Carbon et al., 2010b, 2008a, 2008b; Eidelberg et al., 1998; Trost et al., 2002; Zoons et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The notion that the cerebellum might be involved in some dystonias has been around for decades.
source: Based on patient studies, the notion that the cerebellum might be involved in some dystonias has been around for decades and a number of reports have unequivocally documented that the cerebellum is abnormal in a number of different dystonias (Alarcón et al., 2001; Carbon et al., 2010a; Filip et al., 2013; Jinnah and Hess, 2006; Neychev et al., 2008; Prudente et al., 2014; Simonati et al., 1997; Trost et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: A number of reports have unequivocally documented that the cerebellum is abnormal in a number of different dystonias.
source: Based on patient studies, the notion that the cerebellum might be involved in some dystonias has been around for decades and a number of reports have unequivocally documented that the cerebellum is abnormal in a number of different dystonias (Alarcón et al., 2001; Carbon et al., 2010a; Filip et al., 2013; Jinnah and Hess, 2006; Neychev et al., 2008; Prudente et al., 2014; Simonati et al., 1997; Trost et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: There are clear examples of dystonia in patients that appear to be causally related to cerebellar dysfunction, particularly when dystonia manifests as a symptom in cerebellar-centric disorders such as spinocerebellar or episodic ataxias.
source: Nonetheless there are clear examples of dystonia in patients that appear to be causally related to cerebellar dysfunction, particularly when dystonia manifests as a symptom in cerebellar-centric disorders such as spinocerebellar or episodic ataxias (Bang et al., 2003; Kawarai et al., 2016; Mariotti et al., 2007; Muglan et al., 2016; Nakagaki et al., 2002; Sethi and Jankovic, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: In some cases, lesioning or stimulation of the cerebellum has been documented to improve dystonia symptoms.
source: In some cases, lesioning or stimulation of the cerebellum has been documented to improve the symptoms, corroborating the notion that in some patients, dystonia can arise from cerebellar dysfunction (Koch et al., 2014; Panov et al., 2013; Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: Cerebellar-induced dystonia is associated with bursting cerebellar output.
source: We found, similar to what was noted some twenty years ago in the dystonic rat and more recently in dystonic mouse models of RDP, that cerebellar-induced dystonia is associated with bursting cerebellar output (Fremont et al., 2014, 2015; LeDoux and Lorden, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior studies.

claim: A bursting cerebellar output may be a hallmark of cerebellar-induced dystonia.
source: Our data along with a number of other mouse models of dystonia suggest that a bursting cerebellar output may be a hallmark of cerebellar-induced dystonia (Fremont et al., 2014; LeDoux et al., 1998; LeDoux and Lorden, 1998; Lorden et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to multiple models.

claim: Similar bursting cerebellar output has been documented in a dystonic patient undergoing surgery.
source: Notably, similar bursting cerebellar output has also been documented in a dystonic patient undergoing surgery (Slaughter et al., 1970).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a patient recording.

claim: In the case of cerebellar-induced dystonia animal studies suggest that silencing, lesioning or otherwise normalizing cerebellar output would be an effective therapeutic approach.
source: It is important to note that in the case of cerebellar-induced dystonia animal studies suggest that silencing, lesioning or otherwise normalizing cerebellar output would be an effective therapeutic approach (LeDoux et al., 1993; Neychev et al., 2008), and recent reports document that cerebellar deep brain stimulation and transcranial magnetic stimulation might also be effective in lessening dystonia in patients (Koch et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to animal and patient studies.

claim: Recent reports document that cerebellar deep brain stimulation and transcranial magnetic stimulation might be effective in lessening dystonia in patients.
source: It is important to note that in the case of cerebellar-induced dystonia animal studies suggest that silencing, lesioning or otherwise normalizing cerebellar output would be an effective therapeutic approach (LeDoux et al., 1993; Neychev et al., 2008), and recent reports document that cerebellar deep brain stimulation and transcranial magnetic stimulation might also be effective in lessening dystonia in patients (Koch et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: The disynaptic projection from the cerebellum to the dorsolateral basal ganglia via the thalamus might be the conduit by which the abnormal cerebellar output disrupts basal ganglia function to cause dystonia.
source: Scrutiny of the dystonic mouse model of RDP suggests that the disynaptic projection from the cerebellum to the dorsolateral basal ganglia via the thalamus, which is present both in rodents and nonhuman primates, might be the conduit by which the abnormal cerebellar output disrupts basal ganglia function to cause dystonia (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to the RDP model study.

claim: Severing the link between the cerebellum and basal ganglia by either silencing the relevant thalamic neurons, or lesioning the appropriate region can effectively alleviate cerebellar-induced dystonia in mice.
source: Indeed, severing the link between the cerebellum and basal ganglia by either silencing the relevant thalamic neurons, or lesioning the appropriate region can effectively alleviate cerebellar-induced dystonia in mice (Calderon et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: PNKD, the protein disrupted in paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia was found to play a crucial role in neurotransmitter release by regulating exocytosis.
source: Recently, PNKD, the protein disrupted in paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia was found to play a crucial role in neurotransmitter release by regulating exocytosis (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Several roles for torsinA have been suggested including potential changes in synaptic transmission, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and abnormal levels of eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α) in the dystonic phenotype in DYT1.
source: Several roles for torsinA have been suggested by a number of studies including potential changes in synaptic transmission, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and abnormal levels of eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α) in the dystonic phenotype in DYT1 (Beauvais et al., 2016; Rittiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: The intrinsic activity of both Purkinje cells and DCN neurons are altered by loss of torsinA.
source: Our data provide little mechanistic insight as to the cause of cerebellar dysfunction, although it is clear that at the very least the intrinsic activity of both Purkinje cells and DCN neurons are altered by loss of torsinA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the electrophysiology findings.
